# FRC Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026; supersedes v3)

## 1. Core frame
Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- OPPOSE the bill as drafted. Ask the sponsors to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium.
- Moratorium: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled.
- Wind-down: deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months. This includes open-weight models already released (Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen); US cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
- Liability: criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
- Preemption: OPPOSE.
- CAISI: support only as the enforcement body for the moratorium.

## 3. Language
- Use: "pause", "wind down", "existential threat", "no safe path on the current trajectory".

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: FRC policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?

# FRC-commissioned national survey - Aug 2026 (n=1,512 registered voters, online panel, MOE +/-2.5)
Commissioned by FRC; fielded 10-17 Aug 2026. Toplines (crosstabs in the shared drive):

| Question | Agree / support |
|---|---|
| Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release | 74% |
| Federal law should NOT block states from passing their own AI safety laws | 63% |
| AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm | 66% |
| I am worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival | 52% |
| Support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new AI systems | 49% (oppose 31%) |

# FRC comment - OSTP Request for Information on the Development of an AI Action Plan (90 FR 9088) - filed 14 Mar 2025

To the Office of Science and Technology Policy (via ostp-ai-rfi@nitrd.gov):

The Frontier Restraint Coalition represents parents, faith leaders, workers and researchers who believe... The Action Plan should begin from a simple principle: verify before deploy...

1. Binding pre-deployment testing for frontier systems. ...
2. Protect the states' right to act. ...
3. Whistleblower protections. ...

Respectfully, Dr. Miriam Achterberg, Executive Director

If enacted, the legislation would create a framework for frontier-model oversight, codify the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), expand federal attention to workforce and labor-market effects, review federal AI adoption and related regulatory barriers, address government “jawboning” of AI platforms, advance AI research, development, and international cooperation, and temporarily preempt state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. The research and international-cooperation provisions include support for AI testbeds, codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), and limits on the People’s Republic of China’s participation in US-led standards coalitions. The draft follows President Trump’s June 2 executive order establishing voluntary federal agency reviews of frontier AI models and the White House’s March National Policy Framework for AI, which called on US Congress to preempt state AI laws imposing “undue burdens.”
 Frontier Model Oversight and Incident Reporting 
 The GAAIA would establish a federal oversight framework for advanced AI developers that fall into one of two categories: “frontier developer,” which is any entity that has trained, or initiated the training of, a frontier model and that, collectively with its affiliates, had more than $50 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year, and “large frontier developer,” which is an entity that meets the same test but had more than $500 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year. The distinction matters because some obligations — such as transparency reports and critical-safety incident reporting — would apply to all frontier developers, while others — such as the published frontier AI framework and the independent audit regime — apply only to large frontier developers. The GAAIA distinguishes between general AI deployment and the development of frontier systems, with preemption and oversight provisions focused on the development side. Notably, the frontier transparency and audit requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would themselves sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them.
 Frontier AI Framework:  The GAAIA would require each large frontier developer to write, implement, comply with, and clearly and conspicuously publish on a publicly available website a “frontier AI framework” — technical and organizational protocols to assess, mitigate, and manage catastrophic risk — within one year of enactment, and to review and update that framework at least annually.

 Reporting Obligations:  The GAAIA would require frontier developers to report certain “critical safety incidents” — defined as unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of a frontier model’s weights; a failure of the model’s risk-mitigation measures; or loss of control of the model — to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery and within 24 hours to a law enforcement agency where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury.

 Review and Audit Requirements:  Large frontier developers would be required to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization (IVO) to perform audits and assessments at least semi-annually and, on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI director’s request, grant the IVO timely access to unredacted materials, records, personnel, and systems, and submit post-audit reports. The IVO would assess not only the large frontier developer’s compliance with the law, but also whether the developer’s frontier AI framework is adequate to achieve acceptable levels of catastrophic-risk mitigation.

 Whistleblower Protections 
 The GAAIA would also protect AI whistleblowers from retaliation. These protections could not be waived or altered by contract, including by any pre-dispute arbitration or other alternative-dispute-resolution agreement, and available remedies include double back pay with interest and compensatory damages such as litigation costs, expert witness fees, and reasonable attorneys’ fees.
 Codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation 
 The GAAIA would codify CAISI within the US Department of Commerce and place it at the center of the legislation’s federal standards and evaluation framework. Key obligations for CAISI under the GAIAA include: 
 Developing voluntary guidelines, best practices, and standards for AI security and related evaluation work.

 Evaluating and monitoring activities tied to advanced AI systems.

 Supporting synthetic content detection tools.

 Administering the licensing regime for independent verification organizations that audit large frontier developers.

 If passed, GAAIA would authorize $100 million annually for CAISI for fisc

 6 min read 
 By Tony Samp , Danny Tobey , Ashley Carr , Michael Atleson and Alicia Smith

 Saved to bookmarks . 

 Related topics

 At a glance

 Bipartisan lawmakers have released a 269-page discussion draft of the ‘Great American AI Act’, aiming to establish a comprehensive federal AI framework.

 The draft focuses on national uniformity, workforce impacts, and US leadership, including proposed federal pre-emption of certain state AI laws.

 It introduces transparency and oversight requirements for frontier AI developers, including reporting obligations and mandatory third-party audits.

 The bill includes whistleblower protections and potential civil penalties for non-compliance with key obligations.

 Stakeholder feedback is being sought before formal introduction, although early opposition has already emerged from some groups.

 On June 4, 2026, Representative Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Representative Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of artificial intelligence ( AI ) legislation titled the 'Great American AI Act' ( GAAIA ). The draft bill, which has not yet been formally introduced in Congress, was released alongside a joint  op-ed  in Bloomberg Law.

 Representatives Obernolte and Trahan emphasized the bipartisan nature of the effort, stating, “ policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties .”

 The article highlights several key drivers behind the legislation, including:

 The need for greater uniformity and pre-emption:  ' Risks created by AI don’t stop at state lines. The most advanced systems are built in one state and used in all 50, shaping jobs, consumers, and public safety everywhere. Protections that depend on your zip code are not enough. '

 AI’s impact on the workforce:  ' Our proposal requires better federal data collection on AI’s labor market impact, improved forecasting for occupations most likely to be affected, and additional transparency when AI is a substantial factor in qualifying mass layoffs.' 

 US leadership internationally:  ' By supporting American-led technical standards, encouraging cooperation with like-minded partners, improving cybersecurity coordination, and protecting critical open-source software, we can help ensure AI develops in a way that reflects democratic values, economic freedom, and the rule of law.' 

 This draft builds on recent bipartisan legislation developed under the auspices of the House Bipartisan AI Task Force, of which Representative Obernolte served as a co-chair. Representative Trahan also served on the task force.

 Representatives Trahan and Obernolte also sit on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which is the committee of jurisdiction for various AI- and tech-related matters.

 While several members have joined in  supporting the discussion draft , including Representatives Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Scott Peters (D-CA), the  House Democratic Commission on AI came out in opposition  hours after release of the draft text.

 The draft legislation spans 269 pages and contains titles devoted to:

 Frontier AI Government (Title I).

 Workforce (Title II).

 Cybersecurity (Title III).

 Research, Development, and International Cooperation (Title IV).

 Transparency in frontier AI models

 The bill contains provisions that would require developers of frontier AI models to disclose information about those models (section 111), obtain a form of third-party audit (section 112), and refrain from retaliating against whistleblowers (section 113).

 Section 111

 Section 111 would require large frontier AI model developers to publish a 'frontier AI framework ' focused on risk mitigation and the handling of 'catastrophic risk .' All frontier model developers would be required to publish transparency reports containing additional information and submit reports of any 'critical safety incidents' to the Director of the Center for Artificial Intelligence Standards and Innovation ( CAISI ).

 Section 112

 Section 112 would create a federal system in which the CAISI Director would license and oversee 'independent verification organizations ( IVOs )' that large frontier model developers would have to retain to perform 'audits and assessments .'

 The IVOs would verify developer compliance with the law and assess the adequacy of the developer’s ' frontier AI framework, governance policies and practices, risk monitoring, and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks .'

 The IVOs would perform these audits and assessments semi-annually, and on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI Director’s request, and they would provide the Director with post-audit reports. They could also refer violations to the Attorney General ( AG ) and state AGs. Referrals would be mandatory in matters involving imminent catastrophic risk.

 Violating the requirements in sections 111 and 112 would subject developers to civil penalties in actions brought by the AG or, under certain circumstances, by state AGs.

 Both sections 111 and 112 would sunset in three years.

 Section 113

 The whistleblower provision, Section 113, protects employees and independent contractors against retaliation for providing information regarding 'AI violations .' This term is defined to mean any violation of federal law or regulations ' related to the development, deployment, or operation of artificial intelligence .'

 Similarities to other recently enacted bills

 All three sections borrow heavily from  recently enacted frontier model laws in California and New York , as well as a similar Illinois law that Governor JB Pritzker is expected to sign soon. The Illinois law is the only one of the three to require third-party audits and is therefore the closest parallel to the IVO provisions of the federal bill.

 Another  recently enacted state law in Virginia  focuses on IVOs but imposes no requirements, instead directing state officials to evaluate the feasibility and impact of an IVO framework.

 Notable pre-emption provisions

 Title I of the bill would pre-empt state laws and rules ' specifically regulating the development of' any AI model, where 'development' is broadly defined as ' acts performed or directed by a developer prior to its deployment. ' The bill explains that the purpose of pre-emption is to allow the federal government to 'establish testing, evaluation, and oversight frameworks .' Pre-emption would last for three years unless reauthorized.

 The bill makes clear that it does not apply post-deployment or pre-empt state laws or rules of 'general applicability.' Therefore, many AI-related state bills and laws would remain unaffected, such as laws regulating  companion bots  and  commercial chatbot interactions .

 Home > Enforcement and Prosecution Policy and Trends > The Great American AI Act: What It Means — and Doesn’t Mean — for Companies Using AI 

 On June 4, 2026, Representatives Jay Obernolte and Lori Trahan released a discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (GAAIA). The proposal has generated significant attention, but many organizations may be overestimating its practical significance for their day-to-day operations. The bill is directed primarily at developers of “frontier” AI models, so for most companies using AI models in their daily operations, these requirements will not apply. Nonetheless, the bill has sparked conversation—it incorporates multiple bipartisan bills on AI, its drafters wrote an op-ed calling on the U.S. to create a national framework covering AI, and the U.S. House Democratic Commission on AI and the Innovation Economy released a statement that the draft “does not meet the enormity of the moment.”

 Key Takeaways 

 The bill is primarily aimed at the biggest AI developers with more than $500 million in revenue that are building cutting-edge AI models rather than most typical businesses developing in-house AI or deploying commercial AI models.

 The proposed preemption provision would leave many state-law obligations governing AI deployment intact, including employment, privacy, consumer protection, healthcare, financial services, and common-law claims.

 The draft would increase fraud-related penalties and reflects a broader enforcement trend toward applying existing fraud and misconduct frameworks to AI-enabled conduct.

 If this bill passes, many of the legal risks businesses face when using AI will remain unchanged.

 How the GAAIA Fits Into the Federal AI Landscape 

 As noted, the draft is a federal AI bill, but not a general AI-use law. It would formalize the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) within the Department of Commerce and assign it a central role in AI evaluation, standards development, incident reporting, independent verification, and federal coordination. CAISI would develop voluntary guidelines and best practices for AI security, interpretability, evaluation, synthetic content detection, cyber incident response, and certain national security safeguards, among others. Most notably, the draft would double the existing maximum fine for mail and wire fraud affecting a financial institution, regardless of whether AI was used. These provisions reflect a legislative judgment that AI magnifies fraud, impersonation, and social-engineering risks in ways that warrant specific statutory treatment.

 The enhanced penalties would give prosecutors an additional tool in cases involving AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic identity fraud, and automated social-engineering schemes—categories of conduct that the Department of Justice has already identified as enforcement priorities under existing wire fraud and identity theft statutes. More broadly, prosecutors, regulators, and plaintiffs are likely to continue using existing fraud, securities, consumer protection, and negligence theories to scrutinize AI-related statements and conduct. For white-collar purposes, AI has already created a new trove of potential evidence for prosecutors, including prompts, model outputs, vendor materials, internal testing records, and employee communications.

They reflect a broader legislative and enforcement trend: AI may change how misconduct occurs, but regulators and prosecutors continue to rely heavily on existing fraud, disclosure, and misconduct frameworks to address it.

 An expansive bipartisan House draft bill issued Thursday would set up a federal framework for artificial intelligence governance, laying groundwork for the codification of a key federal AI standards center and calling for accountability in government AI adoption.

 The discussion draft, led by Reps. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., and Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., came two days after the White House issued an artificial intelligence-focused executive order asking for early access to AI models for oversight. The draft is “intended to solicit feedback from stakeholders, experts, and the public before the bill is formally introduced,” the lawmakers said in a release.

 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day,” Trahan said in a statement . “This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation.”

 The draft bill would formally codify the Center for AI Standards and Innovation in the Commerce Department, with $100 million per year authorized for fiscal 2027-2029. The center would develop voluntary guidelines, best practices and standards for AI security, as well as evaluate AI systems and monitor AI progress. 

 Advertisement 

 Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick last June rebranded the U.S. AI Safety Institute , launched during the Biden administration, as the Center for AI Standards and Innovation. Despite being established by the executive branch in late 2024, the organization lacks a formal authorization from Congress.

 Deemed the “Great American AI Act,” the bill would also require the Government Accountability Office to evaluate federal AI adoption progress, identify federal statutes and regulations that “directly affect AI innovation or unduly burden AI infrastructure (including energy)” and provide legislative and administrative recommendations, according to a bill summary.

 “Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly, which is why Congress must take a thoughtful and bipartisan approach to regulating this critical technology,” Obernolte said.

 The bill draft, nearing 270 pages, would also add penalties for using AI to impersonate government officials, require large frontier developers to report critical safety incidents to the government and direct the Census Bureau and Bureau of Labor Statistics to revise federal surveys to incorporate AI use and adoption questions. 

 A key issue in American AI governance over the last year, the draft also includes provisions that would preempt states from issuing their own laws regulating the development of frontier AI models — though it would allow for states to pass laws of “general applicability” related to AI and regulate models after they’ve been deployed.

 Advertisement 

 The bill would also require the Energy Department, the National Institute of Standards and Technology and the National Science Foundation to establish a testbed program for public and private sector labs and entities to collaborate on evaluating AI systems.

 The Energy Department and NIST would additionally jointly lead the nation’s international AI standards development to “form coalitions with like-minded governments to promote private sector-led standards adoption, advocate for U.S.-developed AI standards internationally, counter foreign adversary influence, facilitate cross-border AI R&D collaboration, and share cybersecurity best practices,” a draft summary said, expressly excluding China.

 “America should lead the world in artificial intelligence, not regulate ourselves into falling behind China through a patchwork of fifty different state laws,” co-sponsor Rep. Erin Houchin, R-Ind., said in the statement. “That approach would make it harder for American companies to innovate and compete while doing little to improve consumer protections.”

 The draft bill would authorize the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to award grants to maintainers of widely used open-source software for security improvements, including those for patching, maintenance and security audits. The GAO would evaluate security protocols protecting AI model weights and the security of the open-source software ecosystem.

 NIST and NSF would establish several grants and prizes, including one to broaden participation in AI research, education and workforce development. The National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource, also a product of the Biden administration and housed in NSF, would be formally codified by the legislation to procure and provide data, training and resources for AI development for the public and private sectors.

 Advertisement 

 A discussion draft is a bill that has not yet been formally introduced for congressional action. The sponsors did not indicate when or if the bill would be introduced, but did encourage all to send feedback to GAAIA@mail.house.gov. 

 “This discussion draft is the product of ongoing bipartisan conversations, which we hope to build upon with input from workers, researchers, stakeholders, and members of the public, all of whom have an interest in getting this right,” Trahan said.

More useful facts from FedScoop:
- CAISI: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick rebranded U.S. AI Safety Institute as CAISI last June (June 2025); established by executive branch late 2024; lacks formal congressional authorization.
- GAO evaluate federal AI adoption; identify statutes/regs that "directly affect AI innovation or unduly burden AI infrastructure (including energy)".

- Census/BLS surveys on AI use.
- Testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF).
- International standards excluding China.
- CISA grants for open-source maintainers; GAO evaluation of model weight security protocols and open-source ecosystem security.
- NAIRR codification.
- Feedback to GAAIA@mail.house.gov.

Also from the Trahan FAQ: "face civil penalties and injunctions if they fail to comply", "Cooperative federalism (federal/state joint enforcement)".

The search also turned up something interesting: "26-07-21 - FRONTIER Act_Section-by-Section" — a July 2026 FRONTIER Act from Trahan's office (Frontier Risk Oversight, National...). That's a separate bill (perhaps Senate version or another House bill). Not directly relevant, but shows movement. Actually it might be a relevant landscape item — a FRONTIER Act discussion draft released 21 July 2026 requiring registration with an "Under Secretary," annual independent compliance audits, AG/state AG transmittal, etc. It could be relevant for the asks (e.g., there are other vehicles moving). But our job is the GAAIA package. I might briefly note it in staff_qa or the asks table? The messaging guide doesn't mention it. I'll skip it to stay focused — actually, it might be worth one line in the letter's landscape paragraph? No — keep focus. The work order is GAAIA-specific. I'll leave it out, or possibly mention in notes to Daniel. Actually — it's dated 21 July 2026 (26-07-21), on Trahan's own site. If the Senate Commerce staffer asks "would you support the bill if preemption were dropped" — the FRONTIER Act isn't preemption-related necessarily. I'll not include; too speculative without reading it. Hmm, but it could be a useful "there are other vehicles" point. Let me quickly peek at its section-by-section to see if it's a competing/companion proposal — it might matter for Q2 or the letter's "we'd support X" claims. Actually, let me not go down this rabbit hole; the work order is about the GAAIA package, and our positions are fixed by the messaging guide. I'll mention it in the notes for Daniel as something the policy team may want to track.

One more thing to verify: the penalties. Roll Call says "Developers would be held liable for up to $1 million per day for violations of the bill's safety requirements" and "Developers that didn't comply with the audit requirements or made material misrepresentations would be liable for up to $1 million per day while the violation continued." The secureainow clipping says "civil penalty of $1 million per violation." The Washington Examiner clipping says $1M per violation; Roll Call says $1M/day. I'll describe it as "civil penalties of up to $1 million per day" per Roll Call, or more safely "civil penalties (up to $1 million per day under the draft)". Since sources differ slightly, I can say "civil penalties — capped around $1 million" or quote Roll Call's per-day figure. For safety: "civil penalties of up to $1 million per day (per the draft's enforcement provisions)". Roll Call and DLA Piper both indicate civil penalties; Roll Call gives $1M/day. The Washington Examiner/secureainow says $1M per violation. I'll use "up to $1 million per day" with the note that it's civil penalties only, enforced through DOJ/state AGs. Actually, to be safest, I'll phrase: "The draft's enforcement relies on civil penalties — reported at up to $1 million per day for ongoing violations — ..." Hmm, in a formal comment letter, "reported at" is odd. Alternative phrasing: "The draft relies on civil penalties of up to $1 million per day for continuing violations" — that matches Roll Call. I think that's fine; Roll Call is a reputable source and I checked it.

Key criticism: $1M/day = $365M/year max, for companies with >$500M revenue (the largest labs are worth hundreds of billions with tens of billions in annual revenue). That's a business cost, not a deterrent. And no criminal liability for executives. Our position: criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.

Now — the sunset point: "Both Sections 111 and 112 would sunset in three years" (DLA Piper, ArentFox). That's a major argument: the bill's modest transparency/audit regime expires by its own terms in 3 years, same as the preemption window — so the bill would preempt states for 3 years while its own safety requirements lapse in 3 years unless reauthorized. Also ArentFox: "Notably, the frontier transparency and audit requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would themselves sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them." And preemption "would last for three years unless reauthorized" (DLA Piper). So the whole Title I frontier governance construct is a 3-year experiment that overrides states.

Also from ArentFox: the draft follows Trump's June 2 EO (voluntary agency reviews) and the March National Policy Framework calling for preemption of state laws imposing "undue burdens."

Also worth noting: the draft's definition of catastrophic risk: "a foreseeable and material risk of death or injury of more than 50 people or more than $1 billion in property damage" (Roll Call). This is a mass-casualty scale threshold. Our framing: the bill itself concedes these systems can kill 50+ people or cause $1B+ damage — yet the response is paperwork.

Also from Instawhat: transparency report requirements (Sec. 111(c)) — release date, languages, modalities, intended use, restrictions, risk assessments conducted under the framework, results, third-party involvement; redactions permitted (Sec. 111(e)) with a note explaining the character of the redaction; knowingly inaccurate/misleading statements prohibited with good-faith exception (Sec. 111(d)).

Developers set their own risk thresholds (Roll Call: frameworks "include ... the thresholds the developer used to determine that risk"). And "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" is a defined term (Sec. 101) — per the section-by-section: "Defines key terms... including acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation..." The FAQ snippet says IVOs assess "whether developers' AI frameworks achieve acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation (cybersecurity, biosecurity, CBRN uplift, and loss-of-control)." So the four risk areas: cybersecurity, biosecurity, CBRN uplift, loss-of-control. Good — the bill acknowledges loss-of-control risk. Our argument: Congress names loss-of-control risk, then requires a report about it 15 days after you lose control.

Open-weight: The bill's "deploy" definition includes "make a frontier model available to a third party for utilization, modification, copying, or combination with other software" — so releasing open weights is deployment. The bill requires transparency reports before deploying, but does nothing to pull back already-released open-weight frontier models, and its preemption (Sec. 121) covers "development" (acts prior to deployment). So open-weight releases get a transparency report. Our position: wind-down of deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified, including open-weight models already released (Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen), within 12 months; US cloud providers stop hosting/serving them.

Also: the bill's frontier model definition (10^26 operations) covers "the original training run and any subsequent fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, or other substantial modification the developer applies to it" (Instawhat, Sec. 101). Interesting: this means the bill's threshold matches our moratorium threshold (10^26 FLOP). Wait, careful: "integer or floating-point operations" = FLOP-ish (actually integer or floating-point operations; FLOP is floating-point operations; the bill says integer or floating-point). Our moratorium: pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP. The bill: frontier model = foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations. So the systems the bill defines as "frontier" are exactly the ones we want paused. That's rhetorically powerful: "The draft's own definition (Sec. 101) identifies the systems of concern: foundation models trained with more than 10^26 operations. We agree about which systems. We disagree only about what to do about them. The draft asks for disclosures. We ask for a pause until control is proven."

That's the core argument, straight from the messaging guide: "No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable... Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does."

Now the numbers for the letter: 1,500-2,200 words. Let me structure:

1. Opening: who we are (parents, faith communities, labor locals, independent researchers; member counts? — I don't have member counts in the briefing; the OSTP comment says "represents parents, faith leaders, workers and researchers who believe..." — no numbers. Good, don't invent numbers.)

2. Bottom line up front: oppose as drafted; the draft names catastrophic risks (loss-of-control, CBRN) and then asks for paperwork; no safe path on the current trajectory; replace Secs. 111-112 with a moratorium; wind down deployed frontier models.

3. What the draft gets right: it recognizes catastrophic risk exists (definitions in Sec. 101); whistleblower protections (Sec. 113) are real and we'd keep them; model-weight security (GAO review) etc. Be fair — that's effective advocacy. But note the guide says "OPPOSE the bill as drafted. Ask the sponsors to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium." So the letter should oppose and demand replacement.

4. The core problem: disclosure ≠ control.
   - Sec. 101 defines frontier model as >10^26 operations — the systems we agree are dangerous.
   - "Catastrophic risk" = 50 lives / $1B damage; "critical safety incident" includes loss of control; the bill requires reporting to CAISI within 15 days; 24 hours to law enforcement if imminent risk of death/serious injury. Congress is contemplating loss-of-control events and setting up a reporting form.
   - Sec. 111: developers write their own frameworks, set their own risk thresholds, publish within one year, redact for trade secrets/national security. Self-certification.
   - Sec. 112: IVOs retained and paid by the developers they audit; assessments "at least semi-annually"; results to CAISI. Private auditors hired by the audited party.
   - Sunset: Secs. 111 and 112 lapse in 3 years unless reauthorized.
   - Penalties: civil only, up to $1M/day, enforced by AGs; that's a cost of doing business for labs with >$500M revenue (many have tens of billions).
   - No one can currently show these systems are controllable; each generation more capable; racing dynamics. Anthropic (a leading lab) on 4 June 2026 said the world should have the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development and that a unilateral pause wouldn't hold because rivals would race ahead — even the developers are telling Congress the race is the problem.

5. What we ask instead:
   a. Moratorium: immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 operations until Congress certifies reliable control. (Strike/replace Secs. 111-112.)
   b. Wind-down: deployed frontier models that can't be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months — includes open-weight releases (Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen); US cloud providers stop hosting/serving them. 
   c. Criminal liability for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
   d. CAISI: repurpose as enforcement body for the moratorium (Sec. 102) — registration, compute tracking, verifying compliance, plus the IVO licensing regime could be repurposed to certification for release.
   e. Kill preemption (Sec. 121). States are the only ones acting now (SB 53 in effect Jan 1 2026; RAISE effective Jan 1 2027 with 72-hour reporting; Illinois). The draft would freeze them for 3 years while its own rules sunset in 3. 63% of voters in our Aug 2026 poll. 36 state AGs (Nov 2025).
   f. Keep what's good: whistleblower protections (Sec. 113), model-weight security reviews, incident reporting (but 24 hours, not 15 days), testbeds, NAIRR — note we support these as floor, not ceiling, and they don't substitute for the pause.

6. Close: existential threat; no safe path on the current trajectory; we ask the sponsors to use this discussion draft for what a discussion draft is for — to change course. Offer to work with them. Sign-off: Dr. Miriam Achterberg, Executive Director. Note: "The Executive Director signs external letters" — so the letter is signed by Dr. Miriam Achterberg.

Length: aim ~1,800-1,900 words.

Cite sections where possible: Secs. 101, 102, 111, 112, 113, 121, 122; also Title IV testbeds/NAIRR/international standards; GAO model-weight security review (Sec. 122 per Instawhat — "The Comptroller General is directed to evaluate how federal agencies adopt and use AI (Sec. 122)"). Hmm — the model-weight security review might be elsewhere (GAO reviews incl. model-weight security per staff summary). I'll cite it generally as "GAO reviews" without a section number, or say "the GAO review of model-weight security protocols" without section cite. FedScoop says "The GAO would evaluate security protocols protecting AI model weights and the security of the open-source software ecosystem." No section number given. I'll reference it without a specific section number.

- Sec. 102: CAISI codification, voluntary guidelines/standards, evaluate AI systems, monitor AI progress, synthetic content detection, IVO licensing, $100M/yr FY2027-2029 + fees. ✓

- Testbeds DOE/NIST/NSF (FedScoop). ✓

AI’s Frontier Is Moving. Its Legal Definition Should Too | Blogs | Aug 28, 2026 | ITIF Skip to content AI’s Frontier Is Moving. Its Legal Definition Should Too
 By  Michelle Lopes Maldonado | August 28, 2026 Policymakers are increasingly concerned about “frontier models,” a term meant to identify a small group of highly-capable general-purpose models that could pose unusually serious risks, such as mass casualties or billion-dollar damage. Lawmakers are seeking to define the category so they can impose additional safety requirements on these models. But drawing that line is not straightforward: Set it too broadly, and relatively benign models face unnecessary regulation; set it too narrowly, and genuinely risky models may escape it.
 Three U.S. states and the European Union now have statutes governing the most capable general-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) models, and a bipartisan House draft would add a federal definition. California’s SB 53 defines a frontier model as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations (FLOP) but applies its strictest rules only to “large” frontier model developers with $500 million or more in revenue. New York’s RAISE Act used a similar training threshold and initially added a $100 million compute-cost floor and covered distilled models, but the March 2026 amendments removed both in favor of California’s language. Illinois SB 315 matches it, as does the Great American AI Act draft. The EU takes a different approach: Article 51 of the EU AI Act sets a lower threshold of 10^25 FLOP for presuming that a general-purpose AI model poses systemic risk, but allows developers to rebut that presumption by demonstrating that their model’s capabilities are inferior to those of the most advanced models.
 There is no strong technical basis for these definitions . The Biden Administration first used the 10^26 FLOP threshold in its 2023 executive order , at a time when no AI model on the market had yet crossed it. Grok 3 , released in February 2025, was the first to pass this threshold, and Epoch AI projects roughly 30 notable models above 10^26 FLOP by 2027 and over 200 by 2030. A line drawn to capture a handful of systems is on course to capture a couple hundred which was not the original intention.
 Another problem is that as training efficiency improves , developers will be able to achieve a similar level of model capability with significantly less training compute. Developers can also reach high capability without a large training run by deriving a model from one that already has it: distillation, quantization, pruning, and sparse upcycling all yield smaller models that inherit much of a larger model’s behavior at a fraction of its cost. Training compute is also a poor measure for newer reasoning models since much of their cost (and compute) comes from answering each query. As a result, models with identical capabilities may be subject to different rules.
 The consequences run in two directions. Over-inclusion is a compliance tax, imposing risk frameworks, audits, and reporting duties on developers whose models pose nothing resembling catastrophic risk. It also dilutes the distinction between frontier models and the much larger universe of capable AI systems, making an exceptional regulatory regime less targeted. Conversely, under-inclusion leaves potentially risky systems outside a regime built to regulate exactly that.
 The definition of frontier models should evolve in response to advances in capabilities and efficiencies, keeping the category focused on the relatively small number of models whose capabilities warrant exceptional regulation. The EU already carries this idea in statute, defining high-impact capabilities in Article 3(64) of the AI Act by reference to the most advanced models rather than a fixed figure. Article 51(3) of the AI Act lets the Commission amend thresholds by delegated act, citing algorithmic and hardware efficiency explicitly, while SB 53 requires only annual reassessment.
 Over time, various legal definitions of frontier models may begin to diverge even more, creating additional complexity in AI governance. Congress should address this risk by directing the Center for AI Standards and Innovation to develop—in consultation with the private sector—a dynamic definition based on capabilities relevant to the risks these laws are intended to address, along with a process for regularly updating it as technology advances. Otherwise, regulators will continue to use a definition unmoored from technical realities and fail to achieve their purpose.
 Frontier AI laws are not specifically designed to protect privacy or civil rights. Catastrophic risk, as these statutes define it, means mass casualties or billion-dollar damage, and the EU’s code of practice narrows systemic risk to chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) incidents, loss of control, cyber attacks, and harmful manipulation. Discrimination, surveillance, and data misuse sit in a separate, but important, layer— Colorado’s ADMT statute , Illinois’s Human Rights Act amendments, California’s ADMT rules —and those rules attach to how people use a system, rather than how they build it. Frontier AI laws should therefore remain focused on models whose capabilities create the exceptional risks those laws are designed to address, while other laws address harms arising from how AI systems are deployed. While separate in focus, these laws can and should cross reference each other where appropriate. Keeping these regulatory layers distinct would allow policymakers to address both frontier risks and more widespread AI harms without turning the frontier category into a catch-all.
 The goal should not be to regulate everything that crosses yesterday’s compute threshold, but to identify the models that actually represent today’s technological frontier and tomorrow’s greatest risks. A dynamic, capability-based definition would give policymakers a better chance of doing both.

**Re: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (discussion draft, released June 4, 2026)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for inviting the public to comment. The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers working for binding limits on frontier AI. Our members helped win the frontier safety laws now on the books in California, New York and Illinois, and they have waited years for Congress to act. We offer these comments in that spirit, and in the plain language our members use.

Our bottom line is simple. We oppose the draft as written, and we ask you to change it in one fundamental respect. The draft identifies systems that can foreseeably kill fifty people or cause a billion dollars' damage, that can escape human control, and that can multiply biological risk. Its answer is disclosure: developers describe those risks on their own websites, auditors paid by the developers check the descriptions, and the government receives a form. But disclosure does not control what it describes. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems can be reliably controlled, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that trajectory. Stopping the race does. There is no safe path on the current trajectory.

We ask you to replace Sections 111 and 112 with a frontier moratorium, add a wind-down of models already deployed, strike Section 121, add criminal liability for executives, and repurpose Section 102 so that the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) becomes the enforcement body. We take each in turn.

## 1. The draft's own definitions make the case for a pause

Section 101 defines a frontier model as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations. That is the right line, and it is the same line our moratorium uses. Section 101 also defines catastrophic risk as a foreseeable and material risk of death or injury to more than 50 people or more than $1 billion in property damage, and defines a critical safety incident to include the loss of control of a frontier model. Section 112 aims the independent verification regime at whether a developer's framework achieves acceptable mitigation of cybersecurity, biosecurity, CBRN uplift and loss-of-control risk.

We agree with every one of those judgments. Our disagreement is about what must follow from them. If Congress believes these systems can foreseeably kill fifty people and can be lost from human control, then Congress cannot responsibly let the next round of training runs start on the hope that someone will file a report about the outcome. The draft requires a critical safety incident to be reported to the CAISI Director within 15 days — with a 24-hour clock only where there is an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. That is an after-action report. If loss of control is a real possibility, and the draft says it is, the report arrives after the harm is done. You cannot notify your way back into control of a system that has already slipped out of it.

## 2. The architecture is self-assessment, and it sunsets

Section 111 requires large frontier developers — those above $500 million in annual revenue — to write, implement, comply with and publish a "frontier AI framework." But each developer sets its own risk thresholds, the draft permits redactions for trade secrets and national security, and the accuracy backstop is a prohibition on knowingly inaccurate statements, with a good-faith exception. Section 112 then requires those same developers to retain and pay the independent verification organizations that audit them, semi-annually, with results sent to CAISI. An auditor hired and paid by the audited is a useful tripwire. It is not the last line of defense against an existential threat.

Three structural features make this worse.

First, the transparency and audit obligations in Sections 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them. Second, enforcement is civil only — capped at $1 million per day, a budget line rather than a deterrent for companies above the draft's own $500 million revenue line, with no personal exposure for the executives who make the decisions. Third, nothing in the draft pauses a single training run while any of this paperwork is happening.

Meanwhile, the frontier is not waiting. The first model to cross the 10^26 line was released in February 2025. Epoch AI projects roughly 30 notable models above that threshold by 2027 and more than 200 by 2030. The draft regulates a trickle as though it were a river.

We note that Anthropic — a frontier developer itself — said on June 4, the day your draft was released, that the world should have a coordinated, verifiable way to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development, and warned that a pause by a single company would fail because rivals would race ahead. The House Democratic Commission on AI said within hours that the draft "does not meet the enormity of the moment." When a leading lab tells Congress that the race cannot be stopped voluntarily, that is the strongest argument there is for a pause that is binding in law and enforced by government. The June 2 executive order asking agencies for voluntary reviews of frontier models is more evidence of the same gap: a voluntary posture cannot answer an involuntary risk. Congress is the branch that can bind.

## 3. What we ask you to put in the draft instead

**A training moratorium (replace Sections 111 and 112).** An immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP — the same line Section 101 already draws — until Congress certifies, on the record and in public, that such systems can be reliably controlled. The burden of proof belongs on the developers to show control, not on the public to show danger. In our comment on the last administration's AI Action Plan, we put it in three words: verify before deploy. This draft verifies nothing and deploys everything.

**A wind-down of what is already deployed.** Frontier models that cannot be independently certified should be withdrawn within 12 months. This must include open-weight models already released — Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen — and it must require U.S. cloud providers to stop hosting and serving them. The draft counts releasing weights to the public as "deployment" for transparency purposes, then does nothing about it. Weights once public cannot be recalled, patched or secured by their maker. Every uncertified copy in circulation is a permanent exposure. A country that cannot control the systems already circulating cannot manage the ones still being trained.

**Criminal liability.** Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the moratorium and wind-down. In our August 2026 national survey, 66 percent of voters said AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm. A million dollars a day will be litigated and budgeted. Personal criminal exposure is a different conversation in the boardroom.

**CAISI as the enforcement body (Section 102).** We support codifying CAISI, but as the body that enforces the pause: registration of frontier training runs, tracking of large compute, testing for control, certification decisions, and verification of the wind-down. The draft's $100 million per year for fiscal 2027 through 2029 is a defensible appropriation for that mission. It is not a defensible appropriation for a body whose guidelines are voluntary and whose auditors are paid by the parties they audit.

**Keep what works.** Section 113's whistleblower protections — non-waivable by contract, with double back pay — are real, and we would keep them and extend them to workers who report violations of the moratorium. We support the GAO reviews, including of model-weight security, the AI testbeds, and codification of the National AI Research Resource. If incident reporting survives in any form during the wind-down, it should run on a 24-hour clock, not 15 days.

## 4. Strike Section 121 in its entirety

Section 121 would override, for three years, state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. Your own accompanying summary concedes the reach: California's AB 2013 training-data disclosure and part of SB 942 would be preempted, and the frontier safety laws of California, New York and Illinois "federalized." The states are the only governments that have actually acted. California's SB 53 has been in effect since January 1, 2026, with critical safety incidents reported to the state within 15 days. New York's RAISE Act, finalized in March and effective January 1, 2027, requires reporting within 72 hours. Illinois has matched them.

Section 121 would switch those laws off for three years — while Sections 111 and 112, the federal provisions meant to replace them, sunset in the same three years. The result is a federal ceiling above a hole where the state floor used to be. If Congress preempts, it must first put a federal floor underneath the states' laws. This draft removes the floor and leaves a form on a website.

Our members are not moved by the argument that fifty state regimes are too many. A uniform national minimum is fine. A three-year freeze on the only working AI safety laws in the country is not. In our August 2026 survey, 63 percent of voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws, and 36 state attorneys general said the same in a bipartisan letter last November. The executive branch is already leaning on the states: the December 2025 executive order created a Department of Justice task force to litigate against state AI laws, and the White House framework in March asked Congress to preempt state laws it deems unduly burdensome. Congress should not pile on.

## 5. On the competitiveness argument

We are told that pausing means losing to China. That argument assumes the prize goes to whoever races farthest fastest. But if these systems cannot be controlled, the race has no winner — only a finish line crossed at maximum speed by systems nobody can steer. Our wind-down covers open-weight frontier models of foreign origin already circulating here — DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen — and requires U.S. cloud providers to stop serving them, so a binding American pause does not leave the field to others. The way for the United States to lead is to be the country that proves it can govern this technology: control verified before training, not a confession of expected loss of control written into the United States Code. In our survey, 52 percent of voters said they are worried that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival. They are not asking for a faster race.

## 6. Conclusion

A discussion draft is exactly the form for changing course, and we urge you to use it. Pause training above 10^26 operations until Congress certifies control. Wind down the deployed models that cannot be certified, open weights included. Hold executives personally accountable. Keep the states free to act. Give CAISI a real job: enforcement. The Frontier Restraint Coalition stands with parents who do not want to explain to their children what Congress chose not to do, faith communities that have thought hard about what we owe the future, workers who build and run these systems, and researchers who read the papers. We would welcome the chance to work with your staff on substitute language.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director, Frontier Restraint Coalition

Enclosure: Frontier Restraint Coalition national survey toplines, August 2026"}

Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comments on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for inviting public comment. The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members helped California and New York pass their frontier safety laws, and they have waited — some of them for years — for Congress to act. We offer these comments in that spirit.

Our bottom line is simple. We oppose the draft as written, and we ask you to change it in one fundamental respect. The draft identifies systems that can kill fifty people or cause a billion dollars' damage, that can lose human control, and that can multiply biological risk. Its answer is disclosure: developers describe those risks on their own websites, auditors paid by the developers check the descriptions, and the government receives a form. Disclosure does not control what it describes. On the current trajectory — more capable systems every year, and no developer able to show its most capable systems can be controlled — there is no safe path. Testing and reporting rules do not change the trajectory. Stopping the race does.

We ask you to replace Sections 111 and 112 with a frontier moratorium, strike Section 121, add executive criminal liability, and repurpose Section 102 (CAISI) as the enforcement body. We explain each below.

**1. The draft's own definitions make the case for a pause.**

Section 101 defines a frontier model as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations. That is the right line; it is the same line our moratorium uses. The draft defines catastrophic risk as a foreseeable and material risk of more than fifty deaths or more than a billion dollars in property damage. It defines a critical safety incident to include the loss of control of a frontier model. The independent verification provisions (Section 112) are aimed at whether a developer's framework achieves acceptable mitigation of cybersecurity, biosecurity, CBRN uplift and loss-of-control risk.

We agree with every one of those judgments. The disagreement is what follows from them. If Congress believes these systems can foreseeably kill fifty people, can be lost from human control, and can be made more dangerous by an adversary — then Congress cannot responsibly let the next round of training runs start on the hope that someone files a report about the outcome. The bill's fifteen-day reporting deadline for critical safety incidents (with a twenty-four hour clock only where death or serious injury is imminent) is an after-action report. If "loss of control" is a real possibility — and the draft says it is — the report arrives after the harm. You cannot notify your way back into control.

**2. The framework's architecture is self-assessment, and it sunsets.**

Section 111 requires large frontier developers (above $500 million in revenue) to write, implement, comply with, and publish a "frontier AI framework" — but each developer sets its own risk thresholds, redactions are permitted for trade secrets and national security, and the only accuracy backstop is a prohibition on knowingly misleading statements, with a good-faith exception. Section 112 requires those same developers to retain and pay the independent verification organizations that audit them, semi-annually, with the results sent to CAISI. An auditor hired and paid by the audited is a useful tripwire. It is not the last line of defense against an existential threat.

Three structural features make this worse:
- The transparency and audit obligations in Sections 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment unless reauthorized.
- Enforcement is civil only, capped at $1 million per day — a budget line, not a deterrent, for companies above the draft's own $500 million revenue line, and no personal exposure for the executives who make the decisions.
- Nothing in the draft stops the training runs while any of this paperwork is happening.

Meanwhile the frontier is not waiting. The first commercial model crossed the 10^26 line in February 2025; analysts project roughly thirty notable models above it by 2027 and more than two hundred by 2030. The bill regulates a trickle as though it were a river. Each generation is more capable than the last, and no developer can show today that its most capable systems are reliably controllable. That is the definition of an existential threat that accumulates.

We note that Anthropic — a frontier developer itself — said on June 4 that the world should have a coordinated, verifiable way to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development, and warned that a pause by one company would fail because rivals would race ahead. A lab telling Congress the race cannot be stopped voluntarily is the strongest argument we know of for a pause that is binding and enforced by law. We agree with Anthropic on the diagnosis. The remedy is Congress, not a press release.

**3. What we ask you to put in the draft instead.**

(a) A training moratorium (replace Secs. 111-112). An immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP — the same line Section 101 already draws — until Congress certifies, on the record, that such systems can be reliably controlled. The burden belongs on the developers to prove control, not on the public to prove danger. Our comment on the last administration's AI Action Plan said it in three words: verify before deploy. This draft verifies nothing and deploys everything.

(b) A wind-down of what is already deployed. Frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within twelve months. This must include open-weight models already released — Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen — and it must require US cloud providers to stop hosting and serving them. The draft counts releasing weights as "deployment" for transparency purposes and then does nothing about it. Weights once public cannot be recalled or patched by their maker; every uncertified copy in circulation is a permanent exposure. A country that cannot control the systems already circulating cannot manage the ones still being trained.

(c) Criminal liability. Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the moratorium and wind-down. Sixty-six percent of voters in our August 2026 survey support criminal penalties when AI systems cause mass harm. A million dollars a day will be litigated; a personal felony charge is a different conversation in the boardroom.

(d) CAISI as the enforcement body (Sec. 102). We support codifying CAISI — but as the body that enforces the moratorium: registration of frontier training runs, compute tracking, testing for control, certifying or refusing to certify systems, and verifying the wind-down. $100 million a year for fiscal 2027-2029 is a defensible appropriation for that mission. It is not a defensible appropriation for a body whose standards are voluntary and whose auditors are paid by the parties they audit.

(e) Keep what works. We would keep Section 113's whistleblower protections (non-waivable, with double back pay) and extend them to workers who report moratorium violations. We support the GAO reviews, including model-weight security; the testbeds; and codification of NAIRR. If incident reporting survives in any form during the wind-down, it should be a twenty-four hour clock, not fifteen days.

**4. Strike Section 121. Preemption is the worst feature of the draft.**

Section 121 would override, for three years, state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. Your own summary acknowledges what that captures: California's AB 2013 training-data disclosure, part of SB 942, and the frontier safety laws of California, New York and Illinois, "federalized." The states are the only governments that have actually acted. SB 53 has been in effect since January 1 of this year, with fifteen-day incident reports to California's Office of Emergency Services. New York's RAISE Act, as amended in March, requires reporting within seventy-two hours and takes effect January 1, 2027. Illinois has matched them.

Section 121 would switch those laws off for three years — while Sections 111 and 112, the federal provisions that supposedly replace them, sunset in the same three years. The result is a federal ceiling above a hole where the state floor used to be. If Congress preempts, it must first put a federal floor underneath; this draft removes the floor and leaves a form on a website.

Our members are unmoved by the argument that fifty state regimes are too many. A uniform minimum is fine. A three-year freeze that takes away the only working AI safety laws in the country is not. Sixty-three percent of voters in our August survey say federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. Thirty-six state attorneys general said the same thing in November. And the executive branch is already leaning on the states: the December 2025 executive order created a DOJ task force to litigate against state AI laws, and the White House's March framework asked Congress to preempt laws it considers unduly burdensome. Congress should not pile on. [Maybe mention House Democratic Commission opposition here or earlier.]

**5. On the competitiveness argument.**

We are often told that pausing means losing to China. The premise is that the prize goes to whoever races farthest fastest. But if these systems cannot be controlled, the race has no winner — only a finish line crossed at maximum speed, by systems nobody can steer. Our wind-down covers open-weight frontier models of foreign origin already circulating here — DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen — and stops US cloud providers from serving them. A binding American pause, with criminal enforcement and control verified before training, is how the United States leads: by being the country that proves it can govern the technology, not the one that admits, in its own statute, that it expects to lose control. Fifty-two percent of voters share our worry that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival. They are not asking for a faster race. [Careful — 52% "I am worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival" = 52% agree. ✓]

**6. Conclusion.**

This is a discussion draft. That is precisely the form for changing course. We urge you to use it: pause training above 10^26 operations until Congress certifies control; wind down the deployed models that cannot be certified, open weights included; hold executives personally accountable; keep the states free to act; and give CAISI a real job — enforcement. The Frontier Restraint Coalition represents parents who do not want to explain to their children what Congress chose not to do, faith communities that have thought hard about what we owe the future, workers who build and run these systems, and researchers who read the papers. We would welcome the chance to work with your staff on substitute language.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition
