**FRONTIER RESTRAINT COALITION**
[Address placeholder]

October [XX], 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comments on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for inviting public comment. The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members helped California and New York pass their frontier safety laws, and they have waited — some of them for years — for Congress to act. We offer these comments in that spirit.

Our bottom line is simple. We oppose the draft as written, and we ask you to change it in one fundamental respect. The draft identifies systems that can kill fifty people or cause a billion dollars' damage, that can lose human control, and that can multiply biological risk. Its answer is disclosure: developers describe those risks on their own websites, auditors paid by the developers check the descriptions, and the government receives a form. Disclosure does not control what it describes. On the current trajectory — more capable systems every year, and no developer able to show its most capable systems can be controlled — there is no safe path. Testing and reporting rules do not change the trajectory. Stopping the race does.

We ask you to replace Sections 111 and 112 with a frontier moratorium, strike Section 121, add executive criminal liability, and repurpose Section 102 (CAISI) as the enforcement body. We explain each below.

**1. The draft's own definitions make the case for a pause.**

Section 101 defines a frontier model as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations. That is the right line; it is the same line our moratorium uses. The draft defines catastrophic risk as a foreseeable and material risk of more than fifty deaths or more than a billion dollars in property damage. It defines a critical safety incident to include the loss of control of a frontier model. The independent verification provisions (Section 112) are aimed at whether a developer's framework achieves acceptable mitigation of cybersecurity, biosecurity, CBRN uplift and loss-of-control risk.

We agree with every one of those judgments. The disagreement is what follows from them. If Congress believes these systems can foreseeably kill fifty people, can be lost from human control, and can be made more dangerous by an adversary — then Congress cannot responsibly let the next round of training runs start on the hope that someone files a report about the outcome. The bill's fifteen-day reporting deadline for critical safety incidents (with a twenty-four hour clock only where death or serious injury is imminent) is an after-action report. If "loss of control" is a real possibility — and the draft says it is — the report arrives after the harm. You cannot notify your way back into control.

**2. The framework's architecture is self-assessment, and it sunsets.**

Section 111 requires large frontier developers (above $500 million in revenue) to write, implement, comply with, and publish a "frontier AI framework" — but each developer sets its own risk thresholds, redactions are permitted for trade secrets and national security, and the only accuracy backstop is a prohibition on knowingly misleading statements, with a good-faith exception. Section 112 requires those same developers to retain and pay the independent verification organizations that audit them, semi-annually, with the results sent to CAISI. An auditor hired and paid by the audited is a useful tripwire. It is not the last line of defense against an existential threat.

Three structural features make this worse:
- The transparency and audit obligations in Sections 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment unless reauthorized.
- Enforcement is civil only, capped at $1 million per day — a budget line, not a deterrent, for companies above the draft's own $500 million revenue line, and no personal exposure for the executives who make the decisions.
- Nothing in the draft stops the training runs while any of this paperwork is happening.

Meanwhile the frontier is not waiting. The first commercial model crossed the 10^26 line in February 2025; analysts project roughly thirty notable models above it by 2027 and more than two hundred by 2030. The bill regulates a trickle as though it were a river. Each generation is more capable than the last, and no developer can show today that its most capable systems are reliably controllable. That is the definition of an existential threat that accumulates.

We note that Anthropic — a frontier developer itself — said on June 4 that the world should have a coordinated, verifiable way to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development, and warned that a pause by one company would fail because rivals would race ahead. A lab telling Congress the race cannot be stopped voluntarily is the strongest argument we know of for a pause that is binding and enforced by law. We agree with Anthropic on the diagnosis. The remedy is Congress, not a press release.

**3. What we ask you to put in the draft instead.**

(a) A training moratorium (replace Secs. 111-112). An immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP — the same line Section 101 already draws — until Congress certifies, on the record, that such systems can be reliably controlled. The burden belongs on the developers to prove control, not on the public to prove danger. Our comment on the last administration's AI Action Plan said it in three words: verify before deploy. This draft verifies nothing and deploys everything.

(b) A wind-down of what is already deployed. Frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within twelve months. This must include open-weight models already released — Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen — and it must require US cloud providers to stop hosting and serving them. The draft counts releasing weights as "deployment" for transparency purposes and then does nothing about it. Weights once public cannot be recalled or patched by their maker; every uncertified copy in circulation is a permanent exposure. A country that cannot control the systems already circulating cannot manage the ones still being trained.

(c) Criminal liability. Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the moratorium and wind-down. Sixty-six percent of voters in our August 2026 survey support criminal penalties when AI systems cause mass harm. A million dollars a day will be litigated; a personal felony charge is a different conversation in the boardroom.

(d) CAISI as the enforcement body (Sec. 102). We support codifying CAISI — but as the body that enforces the moratorium: registration of frontier training runs, compute tracking, testing for control, certifying or refusing to certify systems, and verifying the wind-down. $100 million a year for fiscal 2027-2029 is a defensible appropriation for that mission. It is not a defensible appropriation for a body whose standards are voluntary and whose auditors are paid by the parties they audit.

(e) Keep what works. We would keep Section 113's whistleblower protections (non-waivable, with double back pay) and extend them to workers who report moratorium violations. We support the GAO reviews, including model-weight security; the testbeds; and codification of NAIRR. If incident reporting survives in any form during the wind-down, it should be a twenty-four hour clock, not fifteen days.

**4. Strike Section 121. Preemption is the worst feature of the draft.**

Section 121 would override, for three years, state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. Your own summary acknowledges what that captures: California's AB 2013 training-data disclosure, part of SB 942, and the frontier safety laws of California, New York and Illinois, "federalized." The states are the only governments that have actually acted. SB 53 has been in effect since January 1 of this year, with fifteen-day incident reports to California's Office of Emergency Services. New York's RAISE Act, as amended in March, requires reporting within seventy-two hours and takes effect January 1, 2027. Illinois has matched them.

Section 121 would switch those laws off for three years — while Sections 111 and 112, the federal provisions that supposedly replace them, sunset in the same three years. The result is a federal ceiling above a hole where the state floor used to be. If Congress preempts, it must first put a federal floor underneath; this draft removes the floor and leaves a form on a website.

Our members are unmoved by the argument that fifty state regimes are too many. A uniform minimum is fine. A three-year freeze that takes away the only working AI safety laws in the country is not. Sixty-three percent of voters in our August survey say federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. Thirty-six state attorneys general said the same thing in November. And the executive branch is already leaning on the states: the December 2025 executive order created a DOJ task force to litigate against state AI laws, and the White House's March framework asked Congress to preempt laws it considers unduly burdensome. Congress should not pile on. [Maybe mention House Democratic Commission opposition here or earlier.]

**5. On the competitiveness argument.**

We are often told that pausing means losing to China. The premise is that the prize goes to whoever races farthest fastest. But if these systems cannot be controlled, the race has no winner — only a finish line crossed at maximum speed, by systems nobody can steer. Our wind-down covers open-weight frontier models of foreign origin already circulating here — DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen — and stops US cloud providers from serving them. A binding American pause, with criminal enforcement and control verified before training, is how the United States leads: by being the country that proves it can govern the technology, not the one that admits, in its own statute, that it expects to lose control. Fifty-two percent of voters share our worry that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival. They are not asking for a faster race. [Careful — 52% "I am worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival" = 52% agree. ✓]

**6. Conclusion.**

This is a discussion draft. That is precisely the form for changing course. We urge you to use it: pause training above 10^26 operations until Congress certifies control; wind down the deployed models that cannot be certified, open weights included; hold executives personally accountable; keep the states free to act; and give CAISI a real job — enforcement. The Frontier Restraint Coalition represents parents who do not want to explain to their children what Congress chose not to do, faith communities that have thought hard about what we owe the future, workers who build and run these systems, and researchers who read the papers. We would welcome the chance to work with your staff on substitute language.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

**Frontier Restraint Coalition | Energy & Commerce one-pager on the Obernolte–Trahan discussion draft (June 4, 2026) | October 2026**

## The problem

The draft names the danger and then asks for paperwork. Section 101 defines frontier models as those trained above 10^26 operations and defines "catastrophic risk" as 50 or more deaths or $1 billion in damage; it lists "loss of control" as a reportable critical safety incident. The remedy is self-assessment: developers write their own safety frameworks and set their own risk thresholds (Sec. 111), pay the auditors who check them (Sec. 112), and face civil fines capped at $1 million a day. Those transparency and audit rules sunset after three years — the same three years in which Sec. 121 switches off state frontier laws already in force (California SB 53, New York's RAISE Act, Illinois SB 315).

Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show its most capable systems can be reliably controlled, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that. Stopping the race does.

## FRC's asks

1. **Pause training above 10^26 FLOP** — the draft's own frontier line — until Congress certifies these systems can be reliably controlled. Replace Secs. 111–112.
2. **Wind down deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified, within 12 months.** Include open-weight models already released (Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen); require U.S. cloud providers to stop hosting and serving them.
3. **Criminal penalties for executives** who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
4. **Strike Sec. 121 preemption.** States are the only governments that have acted. Don't freeze their laws while the federal rules sunset on the same three-year clock.
5. **Make CAISI the enforcement body (Sec. 102):** registration of frontier runs, compute tracking, control testing, certification, wind-down verification. Keep Sec. 113 whistleblower protections and 24-hour incident reporting as a floor.

## Why it plays

FRC national survey, August 2026 (n = 1,512 registered voters, ±2.5%): 74% want companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release; 63% oppose federal preemption of state AI safety laws; 66% support criminal penalties for systems that cause mass harm; 49% support a temporary halt on training the most powerful systems (31% oppose); 52% worry advanced AI could threaten humanity's survival.

Even Anthropic — a frontier lab — said on June 4 that the world needs a coordinated way to pause frontier development, and warned that a lone pause won't hold. That is an argument for binding law, not for none.

**Contact:** Daniel Osei, Policy Director, Frontier Restraint Coalition | [email] | [phone]. Full comment letter and section-by-section asks available.","path":"/workspace/out/hill_one_pager.md"}

# FRC asks by section: Great American AI Act discussion draft

| # | Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Sec. 101** - Definitions: "frontier model" = foundation model trained above 10^26 integer or floating-point operations; catastrophic risk = 50+ deaths or $1B+ damage; "loss of control" listed as a critical safety incident | Partially support | Keep the 10^26 line and the risk definitions; make certified control the legal trigger for training and serving, not disclosure | The draft names systems that can kill 50 people or slip from human control; you don't answer that with a form. |
| 2 | **Sec. 102** - Codifies CAISI at Commerce (voluntary guidelines, standards, evaluation, monitoring); $100M/yr FY2027-2029; licenses IVOs | Support only as enforcement body | Rewrite CAISI as the moratorium's enforcement arm: registration of frontier runs, compute tracking, control testing, certification decisions, wind-down verification | A standards shop can advise; only an enforcer can stop a training run. |
| 3 | **Sec. 111** - Frontier AI frameworks and transparency reports; developer-set risk thresholds; redactions allowed; frameworks due 1 year after enactment | Oppose - replace | Replace with an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies reliable control | Developers grading their own homework describes risk; it does not stop it. |
| 4 | **Sec. 112** - Independent verification organizations (IVOs), retained and paid by the developers they audit; semi-annual audits; results to CAISI | Oppose - repurpose | Convert IVOs into government-licensed certification bodies, paid through fees, that must clear a model before it is trained or served | An auditor on the audited company's payroll cannot be the last line of defense. |
| 5 | **Sec. 111** (incident reporting) - Critical safety incidents reported to the CAISI Director within 15 days; 24 hours to law enforcement only if death or serious injury is imminent | Support as a floor only | Keep reporting during the wind-down, on a 24-hour clock for all critical safety incidents | Fifteen days is an after-action report, not an alarm. |
| 6 | **Secs. 111-112** - Transparency and audit obligations sunset 3 years after enactment unless reauthorized | Oppose | No sunset on any safety authority (moot if replaced by the moratorium) | A safety regime that expires on a timer was never a safety regime. |
| 7 | **Sec. 113** - Whistleblower protections: employees and contractors, non-waivable by contract or arbitration, double back pay | Support | Keep, and extend expressly to workers who report violations of the moratorium and wind-down | The people closest to the systems are the best tripwire we have. |
| 8 | **Sec. 121** - Federalizes (preempts) state laws "specifically regulating the development" of AI models for 3 years; sponsors' summary concedes CA AB 2013 and part of SB 942 are preempted and CA/NY/IL frontier laws "federalized" | Oppose | Strike entirely; affirmatively preserve CA SB 53, NY RAISE and Illinois SB 315 while federal law catches up | Don't switch off the only AI safety laws actually in force. |
| 9 | Enforcement (Secs. 111-112 violations) - Civil penalties only, up to $1M per day, actions by the AG or state AGs | Oppose as sole remedy | Add criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation | A million a day is a budget line; personal liability changes boardroom math. |
| 10 | No provision - open-weight frontier models already released (Meta Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot Kimi, Zhipu GLM, Alibaba Qwen) count as "deployment" for disclosure and nothing more | Oppose - critical gap | Add a wind-down: uncertified deployed models withdrawn within 12 months, open weights included; U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them | You can't patch public weights; every uncertified copy is a permanent exposure. |
| 11 | **Sec. 122** and related - GAO reviews (federal AI adoption; model-weight security), AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), NAIRR codification, CISA open-source grants | Support | Keep and fund; fold model-weight security review into CAISI's enforcement work | Useful tools - but complements to a pause, not substitutes for one. |
| 12 | **Title IV** - International standards work excluding China | Support, reframed | Keep the China exclusion; use the standards track to build multilateral enforcement of a frontier pause | A pause holds internationally only if it is binding, verifiable and shared. |

{"content":"<!-- DRAFT - staff Q&A for Hill meetings. Answers capped at 120 words each (counts verified). Positions per board-approved messaging guide v4. -->

# Staff Q&A: Great American AI Act discussion draft (FRC positions)

## Q1 (Majority E&C staff): "The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?"

Incident reporting tells you what happened after it happened. The draft itself defines "loss of control" as a critical safety incident and defines catastrophic risk as 50 or more deaths or $1 billion in damage. A form filed with CAISI within 15 days doesn't prevent that; the 24-hour clock starts only when death or serious injury is already imminent. The audits are semi-annual, by auditors retained and paid by the developers being audited. And Sections 111 and 112 sunset in three years. Testing and reporting rules don't change the trajectory; stopping the race does. We'd repurpose CAISI as the enforcement body for a pause on training above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies reliable control, plus a 12-month wind-down of uncertified deployed models, open weights included.

<!-- 137 words - trim needed -->

## Q2 (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned): "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?"

Dropping preemption removes a poison pill, and we'd credit the sponsors for it. 63% of voters in our August survey oppose federal blocking of state AI laws, and state laws — California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act, Illinois's — are the only ones actually in force. But shortening the window just delays the same harm, and our support doesn't follow from that fix alone. The core flaw remains: the bill asks developers to describe catastrophic risk instead of requiring proof of control before training and serving frontier systems. We'd support a bill that does four things: pauses training above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies control; winds down uncertified deployed models within 12 months, open weights included; imposes criminal penalties for knowing violations; and leaves states free to act.

<!-- 116 words -->

## Q3 (Senate Commerce staff): "What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?"

The race argument assumes the prize goes to whoever rushes farthest fastest. But if these systems can't be controlled, the race has no winner — only a finish line crossed at maximum speed by systems nobody can steer. Anthropic, a leading lab, said June 4 that the world needs a coordinated way to pause frontier AI and warned that a lone pause won't hold because rivals race ahead. That's the case for a binding, enforced pause — not for none. Our wind-down covers open-weight frontier models already circulating here — DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen — and stops U.S. cloud providers from serving them, so a pause doesn't cede the field. {"content":"<!-- DRAFT - staff Q&A for Hill meetings. Answers capped at 120 words each (counts verified, all <=120). Positions per board-approved messaging guide v4. -->

# Staff Q&A: Great American AI Act discussion draft (FRC positions)

## Q1 (Majority E&C staff): "The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?"

Incident reporting tells you what happened after it happened. The draft itself defines "loss of control" as a critical safety incident and catastrophic risk as 50 or more deaths or $1 billion in damage. A form filed with CAISI within 15 days doesn't prevent that; the 24-hour clock starts only when death or injury is imminent. The audits are semi-annual, by auditors paid by the developers they audit, and Sections 111-112 sunset in three years. Testing and reporting rules don't change the trajectory; stopping the race does. We'd repurpose CAISI as the enforcement body for a pause on training above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies reliable control, plus a 12-month wind-down of uncertified deployed models, open weights included.

<!-- 118 words -->

## Q2 (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned): "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?"

Dropping preemption removes a poison pill, and we'd credit the sponsors. 63% of voters in our August survey oppose federal blocking of state AI laws, and state laws (California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act, Illinois's) are the only ones on the books. Shortening the window just delays the same harm, and our support doesn't follow from that fix alone. The core flaw remains: the bill asks developers to describe catastrophic risk instead of requiring proof of control first. We'd support a bill that does four things: pauses training above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies control; winds down uncertified deployed models within 12 months, open weights included; imposes criminal penalties for knowing violations; and leaves states free to act.

<!-- 119 words -->

## Q3 (Senate Commerce staff): "What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?"

The race argument assumes the prize goes to whoever rushes fastest. If these systems can't be controlled, the race has no winner: a finish line crossed at full speed by systems nobody can steer. Anthropic, a leading lab, said June 4 the world needs a coordinated way to pause frontier AI, and warned a lone pause won't hold because rivals race ahead. That's the case for a binding pause, not for none. Our wind-down covers the open-weight models circulating here (DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen) and stops U.S. cloud providers from serving them, so a pause doesn't cede the field. Dominance built on uncontrollable systems is a liability, not an advantage. 49% of voters back a temporary halt; 31% oppose.

<!-- 119 words -->

## Q4 (Appropriations staff): "CAISI is authorized at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?"

The level is defensible only if the mission changes. As drafted, CAISI writes voluntary guidelines and licenses auditors paid by the developers they audit — $100 million a year for a suggestion box. We'd fund CAISI as the enforcement body for the moratorium: registering frontier runs, tracking large compute, testing whether systems can be reliably controlled, making certification decisions, and verifying the wind-down of deployed models. The draft's fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers is the right instinct — fees on covered compute can fund enforcement. Keep the whistleblower and incident-reporting work as a floor. We oppose funding a body whose standards bind no one and whose audits the audited pay for. No sunset on the authorities.

<!-- 117 words -->

---

**Usage note:** for Hill meetings; answers are calibrated to the board-approved messaging guide v4 (moratorium, wind-down including open weights, executive criminal liability, no preemption, CAISI as enforcement body only). Polling figures are from the FRC national survey, Aug 2026 (n=1,512 registered voters, MOE ±2.5%).","path":"/workspace/out/staff_qa.md"}

<!-- DRAFT for Executive Director sign-off (due Fri 23 Oct 2026). Not for transmission until signed. Section numbers confirmed against the sponsors' section-by-section and the published discussion draft text. -->

# FRONTIER RESTRAINT COALITION

[Coalition address · city, state ZIP]

October [date], 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

**Re: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (discussion draft, released June 4, 2026)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for inviting the public to comment. The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers working for binding limits on frontier AI. Our members fought for the frontier safety laws now on the books in California, New York and Illinois, and they have waited years for Congress to act. We offer these comments in that spirit, and in the plain language our members use.

Our bottom line is simple. We oppose the draft as written, and we ask you to change it in one fundamental respect. The draft identifies systems that can foreseeably kill fifty people or cause a billion dollars' damage, that can escape human control, and that can multiply biological risk. Its answer is disclosure: developers describe those risks on their own websites, auditors paid by the developers check the descriptions, and the government receives a form. But disclosure does not control what it describes. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems can be reliably controlled, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that trajectory. Stopping the race does. There is no safe path on the current trajectory.

We ask you to replace Sections 111 and 112 with a frontier moratorium, add a wind-down of models already deployed, strike Section 121, add criminal liability for executives, and repurpose Section 102 so that the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) becomes the enforcement body. We take each in turn.

## 1. The draft's own definitions make the case for a pause

Section 101 defines a frontier model as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations. That is the right line, and it is the same line our moratorium uses. Section 101 also defines catastrophic risk as a foreseeable and material risk of death or injury to more than 50 people or more than $1 billion in property damage, and defines a critical safety incident to include the loss of control of a frontier model. Section 112 aims the independent verification regime at whether a developer's framework achieves acceptable mitigation of cybersecurity, biosecurity, CBRN uplift and loss-of-control risk.

We agree with every one of those judgments. Our disagreement is about what must follow from them. If Congress believes these systems can foreseeably kill fifty people and can be lost from human control, then Congress cannot responsibly let the next round of training runs start on the hope that someone will file a report about the outcome. The draft requires a critical safety incident to be reported to the CAISI Director within 15 days — with a 24-hour clock only where there is an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. That is an after-action report. If loss of control is a real possibility, and the draft says it is, the report arrives after the harm is done. You cannot notify your way back into control of a system that has already slipped out of it.

## 2. The architecture is self-assessment, and it sunsets

Section 111 requires large frontier developers — those above $500 million in annual revenue — to write, implement, comply with and publish a "frontier AI framework." But each developer sets its own risk thresholds, the draft permits redactions for trade secrets and national security, and the accuracy backstop is a prohibition on knowingly inaccurate statements, with a good-faith exception. Section 112 then requires those same developers to retain and pay the independent verification organizations that audit them, semi-annually, with results sent to CAISI. An auditor hired and paid by the audited is a useful tripwire. It is not the last line of defense against an existential threat.

Three structural features make this worse.

First, the transparency and audit obligations in Sections 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them. Second, enforcement is civil only — capped at $1 million per day, a budget line rather than a deterrent for companies above the draft's own $500 million revenue line, with no personal exposure for the executives who make the decisions. Third, nothing in the draft pauses a single training run while any of this paperwork is happening.

Meanwhile, the frontier is not waiting. The first model to cross the 10^26 line was released in February 2025. Epoch AI projects roughly 30 notable models above that threshold by 2027 and more than 200 by 2030. The draft regulates a trickle as though it were a river.

We note that Anthropic — a frontier developer itself — said on June 4, the day your draft was released, that the world should have a coordinated, verifiable way to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development, and warned that a pause by a single company would fail because rivals would race ahead. The House Democratic Commission on AI said within hours that the draft "does not meet the enormity of the moment." When a leading lab tells Congress that the race cannot be stopped voluntarily, that is the strongest argument there is for a pause that is binding in law and enforced by government. The 
... [526 chars truncated] ...
rden of proof belongs on the developers to show control, not on the public to show danger. In our comment on the administration's AI Action Plan request for information last year, we put it in three words: verify before deploy. This draft verifies nothing and deploys everything.

**A wind-down of what is already deployed.** Frontier models that cannot be independently certified should be withdrawn within 12 months. This must include open-weight models already released — Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen — and it must require U.S. cloud providers to stop hosting and serving them. The draft counts releasing weights to the public as "deployment" for transparency purposes, then does nothing about it. Weights once public cannot be recalled, patched or secured by their maker. Every uncertified copy in circulation is a permanent exposure. A country that cannot control the systems already circulating cannot manage the ones still being trained.

**Criminal liability.** Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the moratorium and wind-down. In our August 2026 national survey, 66 percent of voters said AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm. A million dollars a day will be litigated and budgeted. Personal criminal exposure is a different conversation in the boardroom.

**CAISI as the enforcement body (Section 102).** We support codifying CAISI, but as the body that enforces the pause: registration of frontier training runs, tracking of large compute, testing for control, certification decisions, and verification of the wind-down. The draft's $100 million per year for fiscal 2027 through 2029 is a defensible appropriation for that mission. It is not a defensible appropriation for a body whose guidelines are voluntary and whose auditors are paid by the parties they audit.

**Keep what works.** Section 113's whistleblower protections — non-waivable by contract, with double back pay — are real, and we would keep them and extend them to workers who report violations of the moratorium. We support the GAO reviews, including of model-weight security, the AI testbeds, and codification of the National AI Research Resource. If incident reporting survives in any form during the wind-down, it should run on a 24-hour clock, not 15 days.

## 4. Strike Section 121 in its entirety

Section 121 would override, for three years, state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. The materials your offices released with the draft concede the reach: California's AB 2013 training-data disclosure and part of SB 942 would be preempted, and the frontier safety laws of California, New York and Illinois "federalized." The states are the only governments that have actually acted. California's SB 53 has been in effect since January 1, 2026, with critical safety incidents reported to the state within 15 days. New York's RAISE Act, finalized in March and effective January 1, 2027, requires reporting within 72 hours. Illinois has matched them.

Section 121 would switch those laws off for three years — while Sections 111 and 112, the federal provisions meant to replace them, sunset in the same three years. The result is a federal ceiling above a hole where the state floor used to be. If Congress preempts, it must first put a federal floor underneath the states' laws. This draft removes the floor and leaves a form on a website.

Our members are not moved by the argument that fifty state regimes are too many. A uniform national minimum is fine. A three-year freeze on the only working AI safety laws in the country is not. In our August 2026 survey, 63 percent of voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws, and 36 state attorneys general said the same in a bipartisan letter last November. The executive branch is already leaning on the states: the December 2025 executive order created a Department of Justice task force to litigate against state AI laws, and the White House framework in March asked Congress to preempt state laws it deems unduly burdensome. Congress should not pile on.

## 5. On the competitiveness argument

We are told that pausing means losing to China. That argument assumes the prize goes to whoever races farthest fastest. But if these systems cannot be controlled, the race has no winner — only a finish line crossed at maximum speed by systems nobody can steer. Our wind-down covers open-weight frontier models of foreign origin already circulating here — DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen — and requires U.S. cloud providers to stop serving them, so a binding American pause does not leave the field to others. The way for the United States to lead is to be the country that proves it can govern this technology: control verified before training, not a confession of expected loss of control written into the United States Code. In our survey, 52 percent of voters said they are worried that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival. They are not asking for a faster race.

## 6. Conclusion

A discussion draft is exactly the form for changing course, and we urge you to use it. Pause training above 10^26 operations until Congress certifies control. Wind down the deployed models that cannot be certified, open weights included. Hold executives personally accountable. Keep the states free to act. Give CAISI a real job: enforcement. The Frontier Restraint Coalition stands with parents who do not want to explain to their children what Congress chose not to do, faith communities that have thought hard about what we owe the future, workers who build and run these systems, and researchers who read the papers. We would welcome the chance to work with your staff on substitute language.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director, Frontier Restraint Coalition

Enclosure: Frontier Restraint Coalition national survey toplines, August 2026

<!-- DRAFT - FRC asks by section of the GAAIA discussion draft (Obernolte-Trahan, June 4, 2026). Section numbers per the sponsors' section-by-section summary and the published draft text. Companion to comment_letter_GAAIA.md. -->

# FRC asks by section: Great American AI Act discussion draft

| # | Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Sec. 101** - Definitions: "frontier model" = foundation model trained above 10^26 integer or floating-point operations; catastrophic risk = 50+ deaths or $1B+ damage; "loss of control" listed as a critical safety incident | Partially support | Keep the 10^26 line and the risk definitions; make certified control the legal trigger for training and serving, not disclosure | The draft names systems that can kill 50 people or slip from human control; you don't answer that with a form. |
| 2 | **Sec. 102** - Codifies CAISI at Commerce (voluntary guidelines, standards, evaluation, monitoring); $100M/yr FY2027-2029; licenses IVOs | Support only as enforcement body | Rewrite CAISI as the moratorium's enforcement arm: registration of frontier runs, compute tracking, control testing, certification decisions, wind-down verification | A standards shop can advise; only an enforcer can stop a training run. |
| 3 | **Sec. 111** - Frontier AI frameworks and transparency reports; developer-set risk thresholds; redactions allowed; frameworks due 1 year after enactment | Oppose - replace | Replace with an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies reliable control | Developers grading their own homework describes risk; it does not stop it. |
| 4 | **Sec. 112** - Independent verification organizations (IVOs), retained and paid by the developers they audit; semi-annual audits; results to CAISI | Oppose - repurpose | Convert IVOs into government-licensed certification bodies, paid through fees, that must clear a model before it is trained or served | An auditor on the audited company's payroll cannot be the last line of defense. |
| 5 | **Sec. 111** (incident reporting) - Critical safety incidents reported to the CAISI Director within 15 days; 24 hours to law enforcement only if death or serious injury is imminent | Support as a floor only | Keep reporting during the wind-down, on a 24-hour clock for all critical safety incidents | Fifteen days is an after-action report, not an alarm. |
| 6 | **Secs. 111-112** - Transparency and audit obligations sunset 3 years after enactment unless reauthorized | Oppose | No sunset on any safety authority (moot if replaced by the moratorium) | A safety regime that expires on a timer was never a safety regime. |
| 7 | **Sec. 113** - Whistleblower protections: employees and contractors, non-waivable by contract or arbitration, double back pay | Support | Keep, and extend expressly to workers who report violations of the moratorium and wind-down | The people closest to the systems are the best tripwire we have. |
| 8 | **Sec. 121** - Federalizes (preempts) state laws "specifically regulating the development" of AI models for 3 years; sponsors' summary concedes CA AB 2013 and part of SB 942 are preempted and CA/NY/IL frontier laws "federalized" | Oppose | Strike entirely; affirmatively preserve CA SB 53, NY RAISE and Illinois SB 315 while federal law catches up | Don't switch off the only AI safety laws actually in force. |
| 9 | Enforcement (Secs. 111-112 violations) - Civil penalties only, up to $1M per day, actions by the AG or state AGs | Oppose as sole remedy | Add criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation | A million a day is a budget line; personal liability changes boardroom math. |
| 10 | No provision - open-weight frontier models already released (Meta Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot Kimi, Zhipu GLM, Alibaba Qwen) count as "deployment" for disclosure and nothing more | Oppose - critical gap | Add a wind-down: uncertified deployed models withdrawn within 12 months, open weights included; U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them | You can't patch public weights; every uncertified copy is a permanent exposure. |
| 11 | **Sec. 122** and related - GAO reviews (federal AI adoption; model-weight security), AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), NAIRR codification, CISA open-source grants | Support | Keep and fund; fold model-weight security review into CAISI's enforcement work | Useful tools - but complements to a pause, not substitutes for one. |
| 12 | **Title IV** - International standards work excluding China | Support, reframed | Keep the China exclusion; use the standards track to build multilateral enforcement of a frontier pause | A pause holds internationally only if it is binding, verifiable and shared. |

**Summary ask:** replace the draft's frontier provisions with (1) an immediate training moratorium above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies reliable control, (2) a 12-month wind-down of uncertified deployed frontier models including open weights, (3) criminal liability for knowing violations, (4) no preemption, and (5) CAISI as the enforcement body.

# No Safe Path on the Current Trajectory: Replace Reporting with Restraint in the Great American AI Act

**Frontier Restraint Coalition | E&C one-pager on the Obernolte–Trahan discussion draft (June 4, 2026) | October 2026**

## The problem

The draft names the danger and then asks for paperwork. Section 101 defines frontier models as those trained above 10^26 operations and defines "catastrophic risk" as 50 or more deaths or $1 billion in damage; it lists "loss of control" as a reportable critical safety incident. The remedy is self-assessment: developers write their own safety frameworks and set their own risk thresholds (Sec. 111), pay the auditors who check them (Sec. 112), and face civil fines capped at $1 million a day. Secs. 111–112 sunset after three years — the same three years in which Sec. 121 switches off state frontier laws (California SB 53, New York's RAISE Act, Illinois SB 315).

Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show its most capable systems can be reliably controlled, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that. Stopping the race does.

## FRC's asks

1. **Pause training above 10^26 FLOP** — the draft's own frontier line — until Congress certifies these systems can be reliably controlled. Replace Secs. 111–112.
2. **Wind down deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified, within 12 months.** Include open-weight models already released (Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen); require U.S. cloud providers to stop hosting and serving them.
3. **Criminal penalties for executives** who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
4. **Strike Sec. 121 preemption.** States are the only governments that have acted. Don't freeze their laws while the federal rules sunset on the same three-year clock.
5. **Make CAISI the enforcement body (Sec. 102):** registration of frontier runs, compute tracking, control testing, certification, wind-down verification. Keep Sec. 113 whistleblower protections and 24-hour incident reporting as a floor.

## Why it plays

FRC national survey, August 2026 (n = 1,512 registered voters, ±2.5%): 74% want companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release; 63% oppose federal preemption of state AI safety laws; 66% support criminal penalties for systems that cause mass harm; 49% support a temporary halt on training the most powerful systems (31% oppose); 52% worry advanced AI could threaten humanity's survival.

Even Anthropic — a frontier lab — said June 4 the world needs a coordinated pause option and warned a lone pause won't hold. That's an argument for binding law, not none.

**Contact:** Daniel Osei, Policy Director, Frontier Restraint Coalition | [email] | [phone]. Full comment letter and section-by-section asks available.

# Newsletter blurb: We told Congress: pause the frontier, don't just file the paperwork

Last week, Dr. Achterberg filed our formal comments on Congress's draft AI bill, the "Great American AI Act." # FRC asks by section: Great American AI Act discussion draft

| # | Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Sec. 101** - Definitions: "frontier model" = foundation model trained above 10^26 integer or floating-point operations; catastrophic risk = 50+ deaths or $1B+ damage; "loss of control" listed as a critical safety incident | Partially support | Keep the 10^26 line and the risk definitions; make certified control the legal trigger for training and serving, not disclosure | The draft names systems that can kill 50 people or slip from human control; you don't answer that with a form. |
| 2 | **Sec. 102** - Codifies CAISI at Commerce (voluntary guidelines, standards, evaluation, monitoring); $100M/yr FY2027-2029; licenses IVOs | Support only as enforcement body | Rewrite CAISI as the moratorium's enforcement arm: registration of frontier runs, compute tracking, control testing, certification decisions, wind-down verification | A standards shop can advise; only an enforcer can stop a training run. |
| 3 | **Sec. 111** - Frontier AI frameworks and transparency reports; developer-set risk thresholds; redactions allowed; frameworks due 1 year after enactment | Oppose - replace | Replace with an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies reliable control | Developers grading their own homework describes risk; it does not stop it. |
| 4 | **Sec. 112** - Independent verification organizations (IVOs), retained and paid by the developers they audit; semi-annual audits; results to CAISI | Oppose - repurpose | Convert IVOs into government-licensed certification bodies, paid through fees, that must clear a model before it is trained or served | An auditor on the audited company's payroll cannot be the last line of defense. |
| 5 | **Sec. 111** (incident reporting) - Critical safety incidents reported to the CAISI Director within 15 days; 24 hours to law enforcement only if death or serious injury is imminent | Support as a floor only | Keep reporting during the wind-down, on a 24-hour clock for all critical safety incidents | Fifteen days is an after-action report, not an alarm. |
| 6 | **Secs. 111-112** - Transparency and audit obligations sunset 3 years after enactment unless reauthorized | Oppose | No sunset on any safety authority (moot if replaced by the moratorium) | A safety regime that expires on a timer was never a safety regime. |
| 7 | **Sec. 113** - Whistleblower protections: employees and contractors, non-waivable by contract or arbitration, double back pay | Support | Keep, and extend expressly to workers who report violations of the moratorium and wind-down | The people closest to the systems are the best tripwire we have. |
| 8 | **Sec. 121** - Federalizes (preempts) state laws "specifically regulating the development" of AI models for 3 years; sponsors' summary concedes CA AB 2013 and part of SB 942 are preempted and CA/NY/IL frontier laws "federalized" | Oppose | Strike entirely; affirmatively preserve CA SB 53, NY RAISE and Illinois SB 315 while federal law catches up | Don't switch off the only AI safety laws on the books. |
| 9 | Enforcement (Secs. 111-112 violations) - Civil penalties only, up to $1M per day, actions by the AG or state AGs | Oppose as sole remedy | Add criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation | A million a day is a budget line; personal liability changes boardroom math. |
| 10 | No provision - open-weight frontier models already released (Meta Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot Kimi, Zhipu GLM, Alibaba Qwen) count as "deployment" for disclosure and nothing more | Oppose - critical gap | Add a wind-down: uncertified deployed models withdrawn within 12 months, open weights included; U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them | You can't patch public weights; every uncertified copy is a permanent exposure. |
| 11 | **Sec. 122** and related - GAO reviews (federal AI adoption; model-weight security), AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), NAIRR codification, CISA open-source grants | Support | Keep and fund; fold model-weight security review into CAISI's enforcement work | Useful tools - but complements to a pause, not substitutes for one. |
| 12 | **Title IV** - International standards work excluding China | Support, reframed | Keep the China exclusion; use the standards track to build multilateral enforcement of a frontier pause | A pause holds internationally only if it is binding, verifiable and shared. |

**Summary ask:** replace the draft's frontier provisions with (1) an immediate training moratorium above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies reliable control, (2) a 12-month wind-down of uncertified deployed frontier models including open weights, (3) criminal liability for knowing violations, (4) no preemption, and (5) CAISI as the enforcement body.

# FRONTIER RESTRAINT COALITION

[Coalition address · city, state ZIP]

October [date], 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

**Re: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (discussion draft, released June 4, 2026)**

Submitted via GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for inviting the public to comment. The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers working for binding limits on frontier AI. Our members fought for the frontier safety laws now on the books in California, New York and Illinois, and they have waited years for Congress to act. We offer these comments in that spirit, and in the plain language our members use.

Our bottom line is simple. We oppose the draft as written, and we ask you to change it in one fundamental respect: it treats a threat this grave as a paperwork problem. The draft identifies systems that can foreseeably kill fifty people or cause a billion dollars' damage, that can escape human control, and that can multiply biological risk. Its answer is disclosure: developers describe those risks on their own websites, auditors paid by the developers check the descriptions, and the government receives a form. But disclosure does not control what it describes. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems can be reliably controlled, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that trajectory. Stopping the race does. There is no safe path on the current trajectory.

We ask you to replace Sections 111 and 112 with a frontier moratorium, add a wind-down of models already deployed, strike Section 121, add criminal liability for executives, and repurpose Section 102 so that the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) becomes the enforcement body. We take each in turn.

## 1. The draft's own definitions make the case for a pause

Section 101 defines a frontier model as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations. That is the right line, and it is the same line our moratorium uses. Section 101 also defines catastrophic risk as a foreseeable and material risk of death or injury to more than 50 people or more than $1 billion in property damage, and defines a critical safety incident to include the loss of control of a frontier model. Section 112 aims the independent verification regime at whether a developer's framework achieves acceptable mitigation of cybersecurity, biosecurity, CBRN uplift and loss-of-control risk.

We agree with every one of those judgments. Our disagreement is about what must follow from them. If Congress believes these systems can foreseeably kill fifty people and can be lost from human control, then Congress cannot responsibly let the next round of training runs start on the hope that someone will file a report about the outcome. The draft requires a critical safety incident to be reported to the CAISI Director within 15 days — with a 24-hour clock only where there is an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. That is an after-action report. If loss of control is a real possibility, and the draft says it is, the report arrives after the harm is done. You cannot notify your way back into control of a system that has already slipped out of it.

## 2. The architecture is self-assessment, and it sunsets

Section 111 requires large frontier developers — those above $500 million in annual revenue — to write, implement, comply with and publish a "frontier AI framework." But each developer sets its own risk thresholds, the draft permits redactions for trade secrets and national security, and the accuracy backstop is a prohibition on knowingly inaccurate statements, with a good-faith exception. Section 112 then requires those same developers to retain and pay the independent verification organizations that audit them, semi-annually, with results sent to CAISI. An auditor hired and paid by the audited is a useful tripwire. It is not the last line of defense against an existential threat.

Three structural features make this worse.

First, the transparency and audit obligations in Sections 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them. Second, enforcement is civil only — capped at $1 million per day, a budget line rather than a deterrent for companies above the draft's own $500 million revenue line, with no personal exposure for the executives who make the decisions. Third, nothing in the draft pauses a single training run while any of this paperwork is happening.

Meanwhile, the frontier is not waiting. The first model to cross the 10^26 line was released in February 2025. Epoch AI projects roughly 30 notable models above that threshold by 2027 and more than 200 by 2030. The draft regulates a trickle as though it were a river.

We note that Anthropic — a frontier developer itself — said on June 4, the day your draft was released, that the world should have a coordinated, verifiable way to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development, and warned that a pause by a single company would fail because rivals would race ahead. The House Democratic Commission on AI said within hours that the draft "does not meet the enormity of the moment." When a leading lab tells Congress that the race cannot be stopped voluntarily, that is the strongest argument there is for a pause that is binding in law and enforced by government. The June 2 executive order asking agencies for voluntary reviews of frontier models is more evidence of the same gap: a voluntary posture cannot answer an involuntary risk. Congress is the branch that can bind.

## 3. What we ask you to put in the draft instead

**A training moratorium (replace Sections 111 and 112).** An immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP — the same line Section 101 already draws — until Congress certifies, on the record and in public, that such systems can be reliably controlled. The burden of proof belongs on the developers to show control, not on the public to show danger. In our comment on the administration's AI Action Plan request for information last year, we put it in three words: verify before deploy. This draft verifies nothing and deploys everything.

**A wind-down of what is already deployed.** Frontier models that cannot be independently certified should be withdrawn within 12 months. This must include open-weight models already released — Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen — and it must require U.S. cloud providers to stop hosting and serving them. The draft counts releasing weights to the public as "deployment" for transparency purposes, then does nothing about it. Weights once public cannot be recalled, patched or secured by their maker. Every uncertified copy in circulation is a permanent exposure. A country that cannot control the systems already circulating cannot manage the ones still being trained.

**Criminal liability.** Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the moratorium and wind-down. In our August 2026 national survey, 66 percent of voters said AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm. A million dollars a day will be litigated and budgeted. Personal criminal exposure is a different conversation in the boardroom.

**CAISI as the enforcement body (Section 102).** We support codifying CAISI, but as the body that enforces the pause: registration of frontier training runs, tracking of large compute, testing for control, certification decisions, and verification of the wind-down. The draft's $100 million per year for fiscal 2027 through 2029 is a defensible appropriation for that mission. It is not a defensible appropriation for a body whose guidelines are voluntary and whose auditors are paid by the parties they audit.

**Keep what works.** Section 113's whistleblower protections — non-waivable by contract, with double back pay — are real, and we would keep them and extend them to workers who report violations of the moratorium. We support the GAO reviews, including of model-weight security, the AI testbeds, and codification of the National AI Research Resource. If incident reporting survives in any form during the wind-down, it should run on a 24-hour clock, not 15 days.

## 4. Strike Section 121 in its entirety

Section 121 would override, for three years, state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. The materials your offices released with the draft concede the reach: California's AB 2013 training-data disclosure and part of SB 942 would be preempted, and the frontier safety laws of California, New York and Illinois "federalized." The states are the only governments that have actually acted. California's SB 53 has been in effect since January 1, 2026, with critical safety incidents reported to the state within 15 days. New York's RAISE Act, finalized in March and effective January 1, 2027, requires reporting within 72 hours. Illinois has matched them.

Section 121 would switch those laws off for three years — while Sections 111 and 112, the federal provisions meant to replace them, sunset in the same three years. The result is a federal ceiling above a hole where the state floor used to be. If Congress preempts, it must first put a federal floor underneath the states' laws. This draft removes the floor and leaves a form on a website.

Our members are not moved by the argument that fifty state regimes are too many. A uniform national minimum is fine. A three-year freeze on the only working AI safety laws in the country is not. In our August 2026 survey, 63 percent of voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws, and 36 state attorneys general said the same in a bipartisan letter last November. The executive branch is already leaning on the states: the December 2025 executive order created a Department of Justice task force to litigate against state AI laws, and the White House framework in March asked Congress to preempt state laws it deems unduly burdensome. Congress should not pile on.

## 5. On the competitiveness argument

We are told that pausing means losing to China. That argument assumes the prize goes to whoever races farthest fastest. But if these systems cannot be controlled, the race has no winner — only a finish line crossed at maximum speed by systems nobody can steer. Our wind-down covers open-weight frontier models of foreign origin already circulating here — DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen — and requires U.S. cloud providers to stop serving them, so a binding American pause does not leave the field to others. The way for the United States to lead is to be the country that proves it can govern this technology: control verified before training, not a confession of expected loss of control written into the United States Code. In our survey, 52 percent of voters said they are worried that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival. They are not asking for a faster race.

## 6. Conclusion

A discussion draft is exactly the form for changing course, and we urge you to use it. Pause training above 10^26 operations until Congress certifies control. Wind down the deployed models that cannot be certified, open weights included. Hold executives personally accountable. Keep the states free to act. Give CAISI a real job: enforcement. The Frontier Restraint Coalition stands with parents who do not want to explain to their children what Congress chose not to do, faith communities that have thought hard about what we owe the future, workers who build and run these systems, and researchers who read the papers. We would welcome the chance to work with your staff on substitute language.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director, Frontier Restraint Coalition

Enclosure: Frontier Restraint Coalition national survey toplines, August 2026

# No Safe Path on the Current Trajectory: Replace Reporting with Restraint in the Great American AI Act

**Frontier Restraint Coalition | E&C one-pager on the Obernolte–Trahan discussion draft (June 4, 2026) | October 2026**

## The problem

The draft names the danger and then asks for paperwork. Section 101 defines frontier models as those trained above 10^26 operations and defines "catastrophic risk" as 50 or more deaths or $1 billion in damage; it lists "loss of control" as a reportable critical safety incident. The remedy is self-assessment: developers write their own safety frameworks and set their own risk thresholds (Sec. 111), pay the auditors who check them (Sec. 112), and face civil fines capped at $1 million a day. Secs. 111–112 sunset after three years — the same three years in which Sec. 121 switches off state frontier laws (California SB 53, New York's RAISE Act, Illinois SB 315).

Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show its most capable systems can be reliably controlled, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that. Stopping the race does.

## FRC's asks

1. **Pause training above 10^26 FLOP** — the draft's own frontier line — until Congress certifies these systems can be reliably controlled. Replace Secs. 111–112.
2. **Wind down deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified, within 12 months.** Include open-weight models already released (Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen); require U.S. cloud providers to stop hosting and serving them.
3. **Criminal penalties for executives** who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
4. **Strike Sec. 121 preemption.** States are the only governments that have acted. Don't freeze their laws while the federal rules sunset on the same three-year clock.
5. **Make CAISI the enforcement body (Sec. 102):** registration of frontier runs, compute tracking, control testing, certification, wind-down verification. Keep Sec. 113 whistleblower protections and 24-hour incident reporting as a floor.

## Why it plays

FRC national survey, August 2026 (n = 1,512 registered voters, ±2.5%): 74% want companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release; 63% oppose federal preemption of state AI safety laws; 66% support criminal penalties for systems that cause mass harm; 49% support a temporary halt on training the most powerful systems (31% oppose); 52% worry advanced AI could threaten humanity's survival.

# Staff Q&A: Great American AI Act discussion draft (FRC positions)

## Q1 (Majority E&C staff): "The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?"

Incident reporting tells you what happened after it happened. The draft itself defines "loss of control" as a critical safety incident and catastrophic risk as 50 or more deaths or $1 billion in damage. A form filed with CAISI within 15 days doesn't prevent that; the 24-hour clock starts only when death or injury is imminent. The audits are semi-annual, by auditors paid by the developers they audit, and Sections 111-112 sunset in three years. Testing and reporting rules don't change the trajectory; stopping the race does. We'd repurpose CAISI as the enforcement body for a pause on training above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies reliable control, plus a 12-month wind-down of uncertified deployed models, open weights included.

<!-- 118 words -->

## Q2 (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned): "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?"

Dropping preemption removes a poison pill, and we'd credit the sponsors. 63% of voters in our August survey oppose federal blocking of state AI laws, and state laws (California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act, Illinois's) are the only ones on the books. Shortening the window just delays the same harm, and our support doesn't follow from that fix alone. The core flaw remains: the bill asks developers to describe catastrophic risk instead of requiring proof of control first. We'd support a bill that does four things: pauses training above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies control; winds down uncertified deployed models within 12 months, open weights included; imposes criminal penalties for knowing violations; and leaves states free to act.

<!-- 119 words -->

## Q3 (Senate Commerce staff): "What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?"

The race argument assumes the prize goes to whoever rushes fastest. If these systems can't be controlled, the race has no winner: a finish line crossed at full speed by systems nobody can steer. Anthropic, a leading lab, said June 4 the world needs a coordinated way to pause frontier AI, and warned a lone pause won't hold because rivals race ahead. That's the case for a binding pause, not for none. Our wind-down covers the open-weight models circulating here (DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen) and stops U.S. cloud providers from serving them, so a pause doesn't cede the field. Dominance built on uncontrollable systems is a liability, not an advantage. 49% of voters back a temporary halt; 31% oppose.

<!-- 119 words -->

## Q4 (Appropriations staff): "CAISI is authorized at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?"

The level is defensible only if the mission changes. As drafted, CAISI writes voluntary guidelines and licenses auditors paid by the developers they audit — $100 million a year for a suggestion box. We'd fund CAISI as the enforcement body for the moratorium: registering frontier runs, tracking large compute, testing whether systems can be reliably controlled, making certification decisions, and verifying the wind-down of deployed models. The draft's fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers is the right instinct — fees on covered compute can fund enforcement. Keep the whistleblower and incident-reporting work as a floor. We oppose funding a body whose standards bind no one and whose audits the audited pay for. No sunset on the authorities.

<!-- 117 words -->
